title: (Scenario) A database query that USED to be fast becomes slow and starts slowing down OTHER, unrelated requests too — why does one slow query drag the whole application down, and how do you fix it? (Every request needs a connection from a small pool, e.g. 10 connections. If one query holds its connection for 10 seconds instead of 50 ms, those connections are tied up, so other requests must WAIT for a free connection — now even fast queries look slow and the whole app feels frozen.)
shortTitle: One slow query drags the whole app down — connection pool exhaustion

s1_definition.profdef: Connection pool exhaustion is a cascading failure where a small number of slow queries each hold their database connection far longer than normal, draining the finite pool so that unrelated, fast requests block waiting to acquire a connection. The symptom is high latency and request pile-up across the whole application, often with low database CPU, because the bottleneck is connection availability, not query compute.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank branch has only ten teller windows (ten connections). Normally each customer is served in fifty seconds and the queue flows. One day a single customer's reconciliation takes ten minutes at a window. One by one, slow customers occupy all ten windows, and now Rajesh, who just wants a fifty-second balance check, stands in a frozen queue. The branch is not out of money or clerks — it is out of free windows.
s1_definition.oneliner: The pool is a shared finite resource, so one slow query that hogs a connection starves every other request behind it.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Connection pool exhaustion is a cascading failure where a small number of slow queries each hold their database connection far longer than normal, draining the finite pool so that unrelated, fast requests block waiting to acquire a connection. The symptom is high latency and request pile-up across the whole application, often with low database CPU, because the bottleneck is connection availability, not query compute.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank branch has only ten teller windows (ten connections). Normally each customer is served in fifty seconds and the queue flows. One day a single customer's reconciliation takes ten minutes at a window. One by one, slow customers occupy all ten windows, and now Rajesh, who just wants a fifty-second balance check, stands in a frozen queue. The branch is not out of money or clerks — it is out of free windows.

**One line to remember:** The pool is a shared finite resource, so one slow query that hogs a connection starves every other request behind it.

sections.s2_technical:
A connection pool like HikariCP keeps a small fixed number of database connections, for example ten, because each connection is expensive on the database side. Every incoming request borrows a connection, runs its query, and returns it. When queries are fast, ten connections easily serve thousands of requests per second because each is held for only milliseconds.

The failure begins when one query's holding time explodes. If a query now takes ten seconds instead of fifty milliseconds — because of a missing index, stale statistics, a lock wait, or data growth — it holds its connection two hundred times longer. A handful of such concurrent queries occupy every connection in the pool.

Once the pool is empty, every new request, even a trivial one, must wait for a connection to be returned. HikariCP will block up to `connectionTimeout` and then throw "Connection is not available, request timed out after 30000ms". Now your logs are full of timeout errors for fast queries that were never slow themselves. The application appears frozen, latency across all endpoints spikes, and requests pile up — yet database CPU is often low, because the connections are idle-waiting on locks, not computing.

To diagnose it: find the slow query first. Use the slow-query log, `pg_stat_activity` to see long-running statements, and your APM. Check HikariCP metrics for connection acquire wait time and look for the "connection not available" messages. Run `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` on the culprit to learn why it got slow.

To minimize the blast radius: fix or add the right index so the query returns to milliseconds. Add a `statement_timeout` at the database and a `@Transactional(timeout = ...)` in the application so one bad query cannot hog a connection indefinitely. Keep transactions short and never make external HTTP calls while holding a connection or a transaction open, because that holds the connection for the duration of the network call. Consider moving heavy analytics or reporting queries to a read replica so they do not compete with normal transactional traffic. Sizing the pool larger is not the primary fix — a bigger pool just delays exhaustion and can overwhelm the database; the real fix is reducing how long each connection is held.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, a reporting endpoint that aggregates yearly transactions used to be quick but became slow after data growth and now takes ten seconds. This is exactly how connection hogging starts — one endpoint holds its connection far too long.

Problem 2 — Rajesh's simple balance check, which takes fifty milliseconds, suddenly times out with "connection not available." This is exactly how pool exhaustion spreads — the fast query is a victim, not the cause, because all ten connections are tied up by the slow report.

Problem 3 — The team's first instinct is to raise the pool from ten to one hundred, but the database then buckles under a hundred heavy queries. This is exactly why pool sizing is not the fix — you must reduce holding time, not increase concurrency.

We will build a `TransferService` with a short, timeout-guarded transaction for normal operations and a separate `ReportService` that routes heavy queries with a query timeout, plus HikariCP configuration showing a sane pool size and connection timeout. We add `@Transactional(timeout = 2)` so a runaway query is cancelled before it can starve the pool.

##### 4b. SQL Database Script

```sql
-- Set a server-side safety net so no statement can run away and hog a connection
-- (applies per session; can also be set per role)
ALTER DATABASE bankdb SET statement_timeout = '3s';

CREATE TABLE accounts (
    account_id  VARCHAR(20) PRIMARY KEY,
    holder_name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    balance     DECIMAL(15,2) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0.00,
    status      VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'ACTIVE'
);

INSERT INTO accounts (account_id, holder_name, balance) VALUES
    ('SAV2001', 'Rajesh Kumar', 1000000.00),
    ('CUR3001', 'Priya Sharma', 250000.00);
```

##### 4c. Configuration File

```yaml
# application.yml
spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/bankdb
    username: bank_app
    password: ${DB_PASSWORD}
    hikari:
      maximum-pool-size: 10        # small, finite pool — this is the shared resource
      connection-timeout: 3000     # fail fast instead of blocking forever
      max-lifetime: 1800000
      leak-detection-threshold: 5000  # warn if a connection is held > 5s
  jpa:
    properties:
      jakarta:
        persistence:
          query:
            timeout: 2000          # cancel a query after 2s
```

# Run
java -jar target/payments-service-1.0.0.jar

# Watch HikariCP pool metrics (exposed via actuator)
curl http://localhost:8080/actuator/metrics/hikaricp.connections.pending

# Find the slow query holding connections
psql bankdb -c "SELECT pid, now()-query_start AS runtime, query FROM pg_stat_activity \
  WHERE state='active' ORDER BY runtime DESC;"
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a pool of ten connections, one slow yearly report query, and many fast balance checks arriving concurrently.

Step 1: Normal state — ten connections serve thousands of fast requests. Each balance check borrows a connection, runs for fifty milliseconds, and returns it. The pool is never empty.

Step 2: The yearly report query degrades to ten seconds after data growth. It borrows a connection and holds it for the full ten seconds.

Step 3: A few more report requests arrive. Each grabs a connection and holds it. Within moments, all ten connections are occupied by slow reports. The pool is now empty.

Step 4: Rajesh's balance check arrives. There is no free connection. HikariCP makes it wait up to the three-second `connection-timeout`. The data at this point is a blocked thread doing nothing useful.

Step 5: The wait expires and HikariCP throws "Connection is not available". The fast query fails even though it was never slow. Across the app, unrelated endpoints pile up and time out. Database CPU is low because connections are stuck waiting, not computing.

Step 6: We apply the fix. `@Transactional(timeout = 2)` cancels any runaway transaction after two seconds and returns its connection. The heavy report is routed to a read replica so it no longer competes with transactional traffic. The pool drains and fast queries flow again.

```
2026-10-25 13:50:20 WARN  HikariPool - bankdb - Connection is not available, request timed out after 3000ms
2026-10-25 13:50:21 INFO  TransferService - Transfer 50000 from SAV2001 to CUR3001 completed
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  HikariCP pool = 10 connections (shared finite resource)

  BEFORE FIX (exhaustion)
    ┌ report1 (10s) ─ holds conn 1 ┐
    ┌ report2 (10s) ─ holds conn 2 ┤
    ...                            ├─ all 10 connections TIED UP
    ┌ report10 (10s) ─ holds conn10┘
                      │
  Rajesh balance check (50ms) ──→ waits for free conn ──→ 3s ──→ TIMEOUT
  (victim, not cause)                                     "connection not available"
  DB CPU: LOW (connections idle-waiting, not computing)

  AFTER FIX
    │ @Transactional(timeout=2) cancels runaway → conn returned in 2s
    │ heavy report → routed to READ REPLICA (own pool)
    │ no external calls inside transaction
    ▼
  Primary pool drains → fast queries acquire instantly → app responsive
```

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ──────────────────────────────┐

  │ ───────────────────────────── │   │ ───────────────────────────── │
  │ @Transactional(timeout=2)     │   │ @Transactional(readOnly,      │
  │ + transfer(from,to,amount)    │   │     timeout=5)                │
  │   NO external calls inside    │   │ + totalSettledForYear(year)   │
  └───────────────────────────────┘   └───────────────────────────────┘

  ── Connection Lifecycle State ──────────────────
  [IDLE in pool] ─borrow─→ [IN USE] ─return─→ [IDLE]
                              │
                      timeout(2s) exceeded
                              ▼
                      [CANCELLED → returned]  (blast radius contained)

  Contract for transfer():
    Pre:  from/to exist, amount > 0
    Post: short txn commits; connection returned within 2s
    Guarantee: a runaway cannot hold a connection indefinitely
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
One slow query drags the whole application down because the database connection pool is a small, shared, finite resource. Every request must borrow a connection from a pool of, say, ten. When queries are fast and held for fifty milliseconds, ten connections serve thousands of requests easily. But if one query starts taking ten seconds, it holds its connection two hundred times longer, and a handful of such queries occupy every connection in the pool. After that, even a trivial balance check cannot get a connection — it waits and then fails with "connection is not available." The fast query becomes a victim, and the whole app appears frozen while database CPU is often low, because the connections are stuck waiting rather than computing.

To diagnose it, I find the slow query first through the slow-query log, pg_stat_activity, and the APM, then I check HikariCP's connection-acquire wait time and look for the "connection not available" messages, and I run EXPLAIN ANALYZE on the culprit to learn why it degraded — usually a missing or ignored index, stale statistics, a lock wait, or data growth.

To minimize the blast radius, I fix the root query, but just as importantly I add guardrails so one bad query can never starve the pool again. I set a statement_timeout at the database and a transaction timeout in the application so a runaway query is cancelled and its connection returned quickly. I keep transactions short and never make external HTTP calls while holding a connection or transaction open. And I move heavy analytics and reporting queries onto a read replica so they stop competing with normal transactional traffic. I deliberately do not just make the pool bigger, because a larger pool only delays exhaustion and can overwhelm the database — the real cure is reducing how long each connection is held.

At the National Bank of India our yearly report endpoint degraded after data growth and started timing out unrelated balance checks even though the database CPU was low. I moved the report to a read replica, added a two-second transaction timeout on the transfer path and a statement timeout on the database, and fixed the underlying index. The pool stopped draining, and fast requests became responsive again. The principle I always repeat is that the connection pool is shared, so protecting its availability protects the entire application.

---

keyPoints: Connection pool: reuse DB connections — avoid create/destroy overhead
HikariCP: fastest Java connection pool (Spring Boot default)
Pool size: too small = thread waiting, too large = DB overloaded
